findings: The primary specimen is identifiable as a Sanderling: a small, plump Calidris shorebird with a rounded body, pale face and underparts, checkered pale-gray/brown upperparts, black legs, and a straight black bill. Its proportions and plumage agree with the attached juvenile and nonbreeding reference photographs.

The primary specimen has one head, one beak, two legs, a short tail, and a normally positioned folded wing; the opposite wing is naturally occluded by the side-profile pose. The feet show the expected three forward toes without an evident hind toe. No duplicated or malformed attached anatomy is visible.

The detached spread-wing and head/bill illustrations read clearly as intentional supplementary studies. The wing study correctly emphasizes the broad white wing stripe, and both depicted bills are straight, dark, mutually consistent, and approximately head-length without truncation or reversed mandibles.
The common name, scientific name, and family are correct: Sanderling, Calidris alba, Scolopacidae.
Every visible descriptive line matches the proposed research text in spelling, numbers, and word order. Habitat, behavior, field marks, and palette labels are complete and intelligible.

The printed measurements—length 18–20 cm, wingspan 35–41 cm, and weight 40–90 g—match Audubon's published ranges. Cornell independently confirms the 18–20 cm length but currently gives a 35 cm wingspan and 40–100 g weight, reflecting source variation rather than a transcription error in this Audubon-based plate.

The ruler is internally consistent: 18 cm is at the bottom, 20 cm at the top, exactly four evenly spaced unlabeled interior ticks divide the range into five proportional segments, and the separate body-length label agrees with it. “SCHEMATIC — NOT TO SCALE” clearly prevents interpreting the printed bird as life-size.

The pale gray-and-white and checkered plumage treatments are supported by the reference photographs and allowed sources: nonbreeding birds are pale gray above and white below, while juveniles have checkered or speckled upperparts. No unsupported seasonal rewrite is required.

The composition cleanly separates the central specimen, measurement graphic, text, anatomical studies, and color swatches. Nothing resembles an unintended additional bird or an anatomical study attached to the primary specimen.
